chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from a freedman of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I saw Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him) call for a cow and slaughter it. When the butchers struck its hocks, it fell to the ground, and they uncovered a part of it.
He said, 'Cut and eat, for indeed Allah, Exalted and Glorious, says, "So when its sides are firmly laid down, eat from it and feed."'
And the sacrificial animal (hady), if it is held in trust (ma'dhun), it is not permissible to eat from it, and that has already passed, and what is narrated adds clarification to it.

key_terms.الْهَدْي: Sacrificial animal offered for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.بَدَنَة: A female cow used for sacrifice
key_terms.عَرَاقِب: The hocks or joints of the legs
key_terms.وَجَبَتْ جُنُوبُهَا: When its sides are firmly laid down (referring to the posture of the animal during slaughter)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating from the sacrificed animal according to Imam al-Hasan al-Awwar?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the practical application of Quranic sacrifice rulings by Imam al-Hasan al-Awwar, who explicitly cited the verse to validate consuming the meat of a slaughtered cow. The narration further clarifies a key jurisprudential distinction: while ordinary slaughtered animals are permissible to eat, the *hady* (sacrificial animal) held in trust (*mamdun*) is not, a point reinforced by the subsequent explanatory text. This underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on distinguishing between general slaughter and specific ritual sacrifices.
